newsitem.title: GERMANY: G7 leaders find consensus in seeking stable dollar.
newsitem.headline: G7 leaders find consensus in seeking stable dollar.

text.p: The world's financial leaders appeared to have found consensus on the desired course of the U.S. dollar on Saturday, almost unanimously proclaiming the view that the strong dollar was now strong enough.

UK Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke told reporters part-way through the discussions between the Group of Seven (G7)finance ministers and central bank governors that the meeting had been productive and agreement had been reached.
Asked whether an agreement had been reached on the dollar, Clarke answered "there has been an agreement, and we will make an announcement in due course."

As they arrived for the meeting, top officials from Germany, Britain, Canada, France, Italy, Japan and the United States had stressed they were comfortable with the dollar's recent gains, noting the rise had been actively sought by the G7.
But they made it equally clear that what was now needed was for exchange rates to remain stable at current levels.
The issue had been expected to dominate the meeting, held in the Kronprinzenpalais, the historic building in which the treaty joining the two halves of Germany was signed in 1990.
The G7's agenda also covers a wide range of themes including the world economic outlook, Europe's single currency plans, debt relief for poor nations and increased bank surveillance.

But the dollar's surge of more than seven percent since the start of the year, seen by some G7 members as potentially destabilising because of the speed of the change, put currency rates firmly on the top of the agenda before the talks.

Comments made before the closing news conferences indicated the G7 would, as expected, announce no specific target for the dollar but would make clear that further gains were not in line with G7 thinking.
Eisuke Sakakibara, director general of the Japanese Ministry of Finance's International Finance Bureau, said the G7 countries had no specific dollar target rate in mind.
But he warned Japan would work with G7 nations to bolster the yen if it fell further. The dollar has risen about 50 percent against the yen in the past two years.
Although there had appeared to be some difference of opinion on the dollar's gains before the meeting, officials arriving in Berlin spoke as with one voice.
Speaking at a breakfast briefing before bilateral meetings with the other officials, German Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer said "the dollar correction process ought to end about now."

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, using the language adopted by the G7 itself to urge the dollar's recovery from all-time lows hit in spring 1995, added "the orderly reversal sought by the G7 has taken place."
Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka made clear that he supported this position.
French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said "I would like the new configuration of foreign exchange rates to be stable and lasting."
The dollar's rise has been particularly good for Europe, boosting exports and lifting growth as countries rush to cut budget deficits in time to launch a single currency in 1999.

It has also helped the United States, keeping import prices low and helping to maintain low inflation in its own economy, though U.S. carmakers are beginning to squeal about the effect the dollar's rise will have on their exports.
But yen weakness, long a boost to Japanese exports, is now beginning to look risky for its financial system.
There are signs the U.S government, a long-time advocate of an ever stronger dollar, views current levels as appropriate.
In a subtle change of tone for the United States, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin noted on Friday the currency had been strong "for some time now."
